code.title: Factory hides the concrete class: swap in a fake

followUps:
Dependency injection is the technique that lets you stop calling new inside business classes: someone else creates the object and hands it in. Creational patterns decide how that object is made; DI decides who makes it and passes it to you.

Example: OrderService(PaymentGateway g) receives the gateway through its constructor. The composition root (or a container) calls a factory or builder once, wires everything, and the service never learns the concrete class. A DI container is basically an automated factory plus a Singleton/Prototype scope manager.

A factory is over-engineering when there is only one implementation and no realistic chance of a second one, or when the object is a plain value. For example new Point(3, 4) or new ArrayList<>() needs no PointFactory.

Wrapping it adds a class, a name to remember and an extra hop when reading, but buys nothing: there is no variation to hide, no setup to centralise and no test fake to swap in. Add the factory later, when a second variant or real setup logic appears; the refactor is small because callers are few.

code.title: Thread-safe lazy Singleton
code.python:
import threading

constructions = 0


class Config:
    _instance = None
    _lock = threading.Lock()

    def __init__(self):
        global constructions
        constructions += 1

    @classmethod
    def get_instance(cls):
        # Double-checked: cheap test first, then test again under the lock.
        if cls._instance is None:
            with cls._lock:
                if cls._instance is None:
                    cls._instance = Config()
        return cls._instance


print("constructions before first use:", constructions)
a = Config.get_instance()
b = Config.get_instance()
print("same instance:", str(a is b).lower())
print("constructions:", constructions)

followUps:
Without volatile, another thread can see a half-built object. instance = new X() is really three steps: allocate memory, run the constructor, assign the reference. The compiler or CPU may reorder so the reference is assigned before the constructor finishes.

Thread A assigns the reference but has not finished the constructor. Thread B does the first, unsynchronised check, sees a non-null reference, skips the lock and uses an object with default (zero or null) fields. volatile forbids that reordering and gives a happens-before edge, so any thread that sees the reference also sees the finished fields.

The class stays unusable and every later access fails. In Java, if the static initialiser of the holder class throws, the JVM marks the class as failed: the first caller gets ExceptionInInitializerError and every later call gets NoClassDefFoundError. The singleton can never be created in that JVM.

With a lazy getInstance() using DCL, the field stays null, so the next call simply tries again, which may be good (transient error) or bad (repeats the failure). Decide deliberately: fail fast at startup, or retry, and log the original cause.

code.title: Singleton guard against a second construction and copies

followUps:
Add a readResolve method that returns the real instance. Java calls it after deserialisation and swaps the freshly built copy for what it returns.

class Registry implements Serializable {
  private static final Registry INSTANCE = new Registry();
  private Registry() {}
  private Object readResolve() { return INSTANCE; }
}

The copy built by readObject is thrown away. For safety, fields should be transient, otherwise an attacker can craft a stream that leaks a reference to the copy before it is replaced.

An enum guarantees one instance per constant by language rules, so it blocks most attacks without extra code. Reflection cannot create one: Constructor.newInstance throws IllegalArgumentException: Cannot reflectively create enum objects.

Serialization writes only the constant's name and reads it back with Enum.valueOf, so you always get the same object. There is no clone (it is final and throws), and the JVM initialises it once, thread-safely. It still does not fix multiple class loaders or multiple JVMs, and it cannot extend another class.

code.title: Global singleton vs injected dependency in tests

followUps:
Migrate in small safe steps, one class at a time, keeping the old static accessor until the last caller is gone.

  1. Extract an interface for the singleton and make it implement it.
  2. Pick one consumer and add a constructor parameter of that interface.
  3. Have the old call site pass Config.getInstance() into it (behaviour unchanged).
  4. Repeat outward until only the composition root calls getInstance().
  5. Make the instance created there and delete the static method.

Tests pass after every step, so each change can ship separately.

No. They share the name but not the rule. Spring's singleton scope means one instance per application context (the container), so two contexts in one JVM have two instances. The GoF Singleton means one instance per class loader, enforced by the class itself with a private constructor.

Spring's bean is an ordinary class: you could still call new on it, and there is no global static accessor; it is injected. That is why it keeps the benefit (one shared object) without the testability problems.

code.title: Simple Factory, Factory Method and Abstract Factory side by side

followUps:
It is a Factory Method. Collection.iterator() is declared in the interface, and each collection (ArrayList, HashSet) overrides it to return its own iterator class. The caller only sees Iterator.

So the creation step is a method that subclasses decide, and the algorithm using the iterator does not know the concrete type. It is not Abstract Factory because one method makes one product, not a family. Similar JDK examples are Calendar.getInstance() and List.of(), which are static factory methods (simple factories).

Replace the switch with a map from key to creator, so adding a new product means adding one map entry instead of editing the factory method.

Map<String, Supplier<Shape>> reg = new HashMap<>();
reg.put("circle", Circle::new);
reg.put("square", Square::new);
Shape s = reg.get(kind).get();

New products register themselves at startup (or through a DI container), so the factory code is closed for modification and open for extension. Reject unknown keys with a clear error.

code.title: Open/Closed factory using a registry

followUps:
Put the plugin classes in a separate JAR, open it with a URLClassLoader (or use ServiceLoader), and register each found implementation in the factory's map.

URL[] urls = { jarPath.toUri().toURL() };
ClassLoader cl = new URLClassLoader(urls, parent);
for (Plugin p : ServiceLoader.load(Plugin.class, cl))
    registry.put(p.key(), p);

The JAR lists its implementations in META-INF/services/<interface>. Keep the class loader reference to unload later, and use a strict interface so plugins cannot reach internals.

Reflection-based factories (Class.forName(name).newInstance()) trade compile-time safety for flexibility. A typo in the string fails only at runtime, refactoring tools cannot see the class, and the constructor must be public and no-arg or you need extra lookups.

They are also slower (small but real), hostile to GraalVM native image and shrinkers unless configured, and a security risk if the class name comes from user input, because it lets attackers instantiate arbitrary classes. Prefer a registry of Suppliers, or ServiceLoader, unless you truly need runtime discovery.

code.title: Abstract Factory: matching families of objects
code.python:
# One factory = one whole family, so storage and queue always match.
class LocalFactory:
    def storage(self): return lambda k: "local-storage:" + k
    def queue(self): return lambda j: "local-queue:" + j


class CloudFactory:
    def storage(self): return lambda k: "cloud-bucket:" + k
    def queue(self): return lambda j: "cloud-topic:" + j


# The client never names a concrete class.
def run(label, factory):
    print(label + ": " + factory.storage()("a.txt") + " | " + factory.queue()("job1"))


run("local", LocalFactory())
run("cloud", CloudFactory())

followUps:
They are close relatives: @Profile picks which set of beans the container builds, and Abstract Factory picks which family of objects a factory returns. In both cases the choice is made once at startup.

Example: under @Profile("prod") you define S3Storage and SqsQueue; under @Profile("test") you define InMemoryStorage and InMemoryQueue. Consumers inject the interfaces and never mix the families. The difference is that the container is the factory, so you write no factory interface yourself.

Abstract Factory is about creating a matching family of objects; Bridge is about separating an abstraction from its implementation so both vary independently. Abstract Factory is a creational pattern, Bridge is structural.

Example: Shape (abstraction) holds a Renderer (implementation): shapes and renderers combine freely at run time. They combine well: an Abstract Factory can build the right Renderer family for the platform and hand it to the Bridge. If you only ask "who makes the objects" it is a factory; if you ask "how do two hierarchies stay independent" it is a Bridge.

code.title: Builder with required field, defaults and validation

followUps:
A step builder forces required steps in order by returning a different interface type after each call, so the compiler refuses to build until every required field is set.

interface UrlStep { MethodStep url(String u); }
interface MethodStep { OptStep method(String m); }
interface OptStep { OptStep timeout(int t); Request build(); }

Request.start().url("x").method("GET").build();

Forgetting url becomes a compile error instead of a runtime exception. The cost is more interfaces, so use it when required fields are many and mistakes are costly.

The Director holds the recipe: a fixed sequence of builder calls that produces a standard product, so callers do not repeat it. For example Director.standardPizza(builder) calls base(), sauce(), cheese() in the right order.

That is useful when the same steps build different representations (an HTML builder and a text builder using one Director). In everyday code a fluent builder is used without a Director, and a named static method such as Request.defaultGet(url) plays the same role.

code.title: Builder mistake: no defensive copy
code.python:
class Order:
    def __init__(self, items):
        self.items = items


shared = ["a", "b"]
bad = Order(shared)             # mistake: keeps the builder's list
own = ["a", "b"]
good = Order(list(own))         # defensive copy
shared.append("c")              # builder reused later
own.append("c")
print("no copy: [" + ", ".join(bad.items) + "]")
print("copy: [" + ", ".join(good.items) + "]")

followUps:
Lombok @Builder generates the builder class and a build() method, but it does not copy collections or validate for you. If the builder stores your List, the product shares it unless you handle it.

Use @Singular on a collection field: Lombok then generates item(x) and items(list) methods and builds an unmodifiable copy in build(). For defaults use @Builder.Default; without it, a field initialiser such as int retries = 3 is ignored by the builder and the value becomes 0. Add checks in your own constructor.

Add a toBuilder() method on the product that creates a builder pre-filled with its current values. Callers then change one field and build a new object, which is the standard way to "modify" an immutable object.

Builder toBuilder() {
    Builder b = new Builder(url);
    b.timeout = timeout;
    b.headers.addAll(headers);   // copy, do not share
    return b;
}

Copy the collections so the new builder cannot change the original. Lombok does the same with @Builder(toBuilder = true).

code.title: Prototype: shallow vs deep copy
code.python:
import copy


class Enemy:
    def __init__(self, name, loot):
        self.name, self.loot = name, loot

    def shallow(self):
        return copy.copy(self)       # shares the list

    def deep(self):
        return copy.deepcopy(self)   # own list


def show(v):
    return "[" + ", ".join(v) + "]"


proto = Enemy("orc", ["sword"])
s = proto.shallow()
s.loot.append("potion")
print("shallow copy added potion -> prototype loot: " + show(proto.loot))
d = proto.deep()
d.loot.append("shield")
print("deep copy added shield -> prototype loot: " + show(proto.loot))
print("deep copy loot: " + show(d.loot))

followUps:
Keep a map from each original object to its copy, and check it before copying anything. When you reach a node that is already in the map, reuse its copy instead of copying again; that stops the infinite loop.

Node copy(Node n, Map<Node,Node> seen) {
  if (seen.containsKey(n)) return seen.get(n);
  Node c = new Node(n.val); seen.put(n, c);
  for (Node x : n.next) c.next.add(copy(x, seen));
  return c;
}

Cost is O(V + E) time and O(V) extra space, and shared references stay shared in the copy.

Cloneable is considered broken because it is a marker interface with no clone() method of its own, and the real Object.clone() is protected. It copies fields without calling a constructor, so invariants are skipped.

It is shallow by default: copying an object with a List field shares the list. Final fields cannot be reassigned in a clone, so deep copying them is impossible, and every subclass must cooperate. A copy constructor or static copy method is safer, shorter and type-checked.

code.title: Shallow vs deep copy of a 2D array
code.python:
grid = [[1, 2], [3, 4]]
shallow = list(grid)                 # copies only the row references
deep = [row[:] for row in grid]      # copies each row too


def show(g):
    return "[" + ", ".join("[" + ", ".join(map(str, r)) + "]" for r in g) + "]"


shallow[0][0] = 7                    # leaks into grid
print("after shallow edit: " + show(grid))
deep[1][1] = 8                       # does not touch grid
print("after deep edit: " + show(grid))
print("deep copy: " + show(deep))

followUps:
Copy each row yourself: int[][].clone() is shallow and copies only the outer array of row references, so the rows are shared.

int[][] deep = new int[g.length][];
for (int i = 0; i < g.length; i++)
    deep[i] = g[i].clone();
// or: Arrays.stream(g).map(int[]::clone).toArray(int[][]::new)

With g = {{1,2},{3,4}}, a shallow clone then c[0][0] = 7 also changes g[0][0]; the deep copy does not. Cost is O(rows x columns) time and space.

List.copyOf returns an unmodifiable list and avoids copying if the argument is already an immutable list from List.of or copyOf. new ArrayList<>(list) always makes a new, modifiable copy.

copyOf rejects null elements (it throws NullPointerException), while ArrayList accepts them. Both are shallow: the elements themselves are shared. Use copyOf for fields you want to expose safely, and ArrayList when you need to modify the copy.

code.title: Connection pool: borrow, release, exhaustion, double return
code.python:
class Pool:
    def __init__(self, max_size):
        self.max, self.created = max_size, 0
        self.idle, self.borrowed = [], set()

    # Real pools block with a timeout; here we return None when exhausted.
    def borrow(self):
        if self.idle:
            c = self.idle.pop()
        elif self.created == self.max:
            return None
        else:
            self.created += 1
            c = f"conn-{self.created}"
        self.borrowed.add(c)
        return c

    # Only a connection we lent out may come back, and only once.
    def release(self, c):
        if c not in self.borrowed:
            return False
        self.borrowed.remove(c)
        self.idle.append(c)
        return True


def b(x): return str(x).lower()


p = Pool(2)
a, c2 = p.borrow(), p.borrow()
print("borrowed " + a)
print("borrowed " + c2)
print("pool exhausted: " + b(p.borrow() is None))
print("released " + a + " -> " + b(p.release(a)))
print("double release -> " + b(p.release(a)))
print("reuse: " + p.borrow())
print("created total: " + str(p.created))

followUps:
HikariCP avoids contention by keeping a fast path that rarely needs a lock. Each thread first checks its own thread-local list of recently used connections, so a thread often gets the connection it used before without contending with others.

If that fails it takes one from a shared ConcurrentBag using compare-and-set state flags (not in use, in use, removed) instead of locks, and only falls back to a hand-off queue when the pool is empty. Waiting threads are handed released connections directly. Fewer locks mean fewer context switches, which matters more than raw speed.

Use Little's Law: connections in use = arrival rate x time per request. Here 2,000 req/s x 0.005 s = 10 connections busy on average.

Add headroom for bursts and slow queries, so about 15 to 20 in total, and compare against the database limit divided by the number of app instances. A bigger pool does not help: past the database's CPU and disk capacity, more connections just queue inside the database. Measure wait time on borrow and adjust.

A humongous allocation in G1 is an object bigger than half a region (regions are 1 to 32 MB). It is placed directly in contiguous old-generation regions, skipping the young generation, and it is freed only by concurrent marking or a full collection.

Many large short-lived arrays (for example 4 MB buffers per request) fragment the heap and trigger extra collections, so reusing a few big buffers from a pool can help. Check with GC logs before pooling, and consider raising the region size first (-XX:G1HeapRegionSize).

Netty keeps big chunks of memory (arenas) and carves them into buffers, so allocating a buffer is just taking a slice and releasing it is giving the slice back. This avoids repeated allocation and garbage collection, especially for direct (off-heap) memory, which is expensive to allocate.

Each thread has a small cache of recently freed buffers, so most requests need no locking. Buffers are reference-counted: you must call release() or you leak memory. The cost of this speed is that mistakes show up as leaks, not as exceptions.

code.title: Mini DI container: singleton vs prototype scope

followUps:
Inject a provider instead of the bean itself, and ask it for a new one each time: ObjectProvider<Task> or Provider<Task> (or @Lookup).

@Service
class Runner {
  private final ObjectProvider<Task> tasks;
  Runner(ObjectProvider<Task> t) { tasks = t; }
  void run() { Task t = tasks.getObject(); }
}

Plain injection happens once when the singleton is built, so the same prototype instance would be reused forever. The provider calls the container again on each getObject(), producing a fresh bean.

Circular dependencies (A needs B, B needs A) mean neither can be fully built first, which signals tangled design. With constructor injection Spring fails at startup with BeanCurrentlyInCreationException; since Spring Boot 2.6 circular references are prohibited by default.

With setter or field injection Spring can use early references and it works, but objects may be seen half-initialised and proxies can differ. Fix the design: extract a third class holding the shared logic, use an event, or invert one dependency. @Lazy is a workaround, not a cure.
